Citi Cuts Bitcoin Price Target Nearly 12% to $99,532, Ether Target to $2,838 Citi, one of the largest U.S. banking groups, cut its base-case price targets for Bitcoin and Ether from $113,000 and $3,028 to $99,532 and $2,838, respectively, representing declines of 11.9% and 6.3%, according to The Block. Citi strategist Alex Saunders cited weakening ETF demand, deleveraging in futures markets, a stronger U.S. dollar, rising real yields and increased equity market volatility as key reasons for the revisions. — link

Highlight Clip: CleanSpark CBO: Bitcoin Mining Will Become Less Profitable Over the Next Decade CleanSpark CBO: Bitcoin Mining Will Become Less Profitable Over the Next Decade CleanSpark Chief Business Officer Harry Sudock said in an interview published by What Bitcoin Did on November 5 that Bitcoin mining will increasingly resemble other commodity industries, with shrinking margins favoring the lowest-cost operators. He expects global hashrate to keep growing over the next decade, but more slowly than in the past ten years. As publicly traded miners shift large facilities toward other uses, mining may no longer depend on listed companies raising billions to build massive sites. Smaller and privately held miners could find more opportunities. Sudock believes the spread of hashrate to regions with cheaper electricity could strengthen Bitcoin's decentralization rather than weaken its security. — link

S&P Maintains USDT Stability Assessment at Lowest Level as Higher-Risk Asset Exposure Rises to 28% S&P Global Ratings maintained its stablecoin stability assessment of Tether's USDT, the world's largest stablecoin, at 5 (weak), the lowest on its five-point scale. The agency said higher-risk assets, including gold, Bitcoin, equities and loans, were equivalent to 28% of USDT in circulation as of September 30, up from 24% a year earlier, raising concerns about potential undercollateralization. S&P also cited limited disclosure of audited financial statements, reserve segregation and custodians. Tether rejected the assessment, saying the problem lies with S&P's framework, not its reserves. — link
